claim: A 2013 CDC report estimates that in the United States, antibiotic resistant infections kill at least 23,000 people each year.
source: A 2013 report from the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 2013) identified the most significant antibiotic resistant pathogens, including S. pneumoniae, extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing Enterobacteriaceae, vancomycin-resistant Enterococci, and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), which has now achieved pandemic spread (Monecke et al., 2011). This report estimates that in the United States, antibiotic resistant infections kill at least 23,000 people each year.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a CDC report from 2013.

claim: A U.K. task force estimates up to 10 million deaths each year due to antibiotic resistant infections world-wide by 2050.
source: A U.K. task force estimates up to 10 million deaths each year due to antibiotic resistant infections world-wide by 2050 (O'Neill, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Neill, 2016.

claim: Some bacteria do not readily acquire new DNA, including pathogenic mycobacteria.
source: However, some bacteria do not readily acquire new DNA, including pathogenic mycobacteria (Musser, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Musser, 1995.

claim: The emergence of antibiotic resistance via mutation can be reduced by ensuring that tissue concentrations of antibiotic always exceed the mutant prevention concentration (MPC).
source: Clinically, the emergence of antibiotic resistance via mutation can be reduced by ensuring that tissue concentrations of antibiotic always exceed a threshold known as the mutant prevention concentration (MPC) (Zhao and Drlica, 2001; Martinez et al., 2012; Drusano, 2004; Baquero and Negri, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to scientific literature.

claim: Above the MPC level, no single mutation can decrease antibiotic sensitivity sufficiently to allow bacterial growth or survival.
source: Above this level, no single mutation can decrease antibiotic sensitivity sufficiently to allow bacterial growth or survival.
evidence: This is a definition of the MPC concept, supported by the preceding citations.

claim: Even concentrations well below the MIC can select for resistant organisms.
source: However, even concentrations well below the MIC can select for resistant organisms (Gullberg et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2011), and the enhanced fitness of even low-level resistant mutants can contribute to the development of high-level resistance (Baquero et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gullberg et al., 2011 and Liu et al., 2011.

claim: The use of antibiotics in combination can limit the emergence of resistance by requiring a bacterium to acquire multiple mutations simultaneously.
source: The use of antibiotics in combination can also limit the emergence of resistance (Mouton, 1999) by requiring a bacterium to acquire multiple mutations simultaneously in order to survive in a multidrug environment (Lipsitch and Levin, 1997; Fischbach, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mouton, 1999; Lipsitch and Levin, 1997; and Fischbach, 2011.

claim: Antibiotic stress can increase mutational frequencies as a direct result of antibiotic action, as seen with the DNA damaging effects of fluoroquinolones.
source: Increased mutational frequencies can be a direct result of antibiotic action, as seen with the DNA damaging effects of fluoroquinolones (Cirz et al., 2005; Cirz and Romesberg, 2006), or due to downstream effects of antibiotics, which have been suggested to involve free radical production resulting in damage to the bacterial chromosome (Kohanski et al., 2010; Foti et al., 2012; Kohanski et al., 2007; Dwyer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cirz et al., 2005 and Cirz and Romesberg, 2006.

claim: Mutation rates can be elevated even by exposure to subinhibitory levels of antibiotic.
source: Recently, several investigators have shown mutation rates can be elevated even by exposure to subinhibitory levels of antibiotic (Monecke et al., 2011; Kohanski et al., 2010; Blázquez et al., 2012; Andersson and Hughes, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: A microtiter-based liquid culture system was developed that enables the isolation of individual antibiotic-resistant mutants while simultaneously monitoring the growth and kill kinetics of the bulk, susceptible population.
source: We developed a microtiter-based liquid culture system that enables the isolation of individual antibiotic-resistant mutants while simultaneously monitoring the growth and kill kinetics of the bulk, susceptible population (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim describes a method developed by the authors and references Figure 1A showing the experimental design.

claim: 384-well plates were uniformly seeded with GFP-expressing M. smegmatis at 10 bacilli per well.
source: We uniformly seeded 384-well plates with green fluorescent protein (GFP)-expressing M. smegmatis (10 bacilli per well), allowed the bacterial populations in each well to expand in parallel for several generations in the manner of Luria and Delbruck (Luria and Delbrück, 1943), and then exposed them to antibiotics.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure performed by the authors.

claim: At the start of antibiotic exposure, the per-well population was sufficiently small so that fluorescent signal in each well was below the threshold of detection, which is approximately 10^5 cells/well.
source: At the start of antibiotic exposure, the per-well population was sufficiently small so that fluorescent signal in each well was below the threshold of detection, which is approximately 105 cells/well (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When M. smegmatis was exposed to ciprofloxacin at 0.3 µg/ml (1.2X MIC), fluorescent signal appeared in 19 of 768 wells.
source: When we exposed M. smegmatis to the FQ ciprofloxacin (CIP) at 0.3 µg/ml (1.2X MIC), we observed the emergence of fluorescent signal in 19 of 768 wells, monitoring fluorescence at daily intervals (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The mutation frequency to ciprofloxacin resistance was 9.7 × 10^-5 based on the peak population of approximately 10^5 bacteria per 384 well plate seen at 12 hr after introduction of CIP.
source: This yields a mutation frequency of 9.7 × 10−5 based on the peak population of approximately 105 bacteria per 384 well plate seen at 12 hr after introduction of CIP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), prior to the onset of killing.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and calculations from the observed bacterial populations.

claim: IC50 increases of isolated ciprofloxacin-resistant clones ranged from 2.2 to 44-fold relative to wild-type.
source: We measured resistance levels of clones cultured from each of the 19 mutants (as IC50, see Materials and methods), and found IC50 increases ranging from a 2.2 to 44-fold relative to wild-type (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: None of the 19 isolated ciprofloxacin-resistant mutants had mutations in gyrA.
source: We thus PCR amplified and sequenced gyrA from each of the 19 isolated mutants, but none had mutations at this locus.
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data obtained by the authors.

claim: Whole genome sequencing revealed resistance-conferring mutations in the lfrR gene in four mutants (21%).
source: We then performed whole genome sequencing (WGS, Table 1) of each mutant, which revealed resistance-conferring mutations in the lfrR gene in four mutants (21%).
evidence: The claim is based on whole genome sequencing data presented in Table 1.

claim: The lfrR gene encodes a transcriptional repressor of the LfrA efflux pump.
source: The lfrR gene encodes a transcriptional repressor of the LfrA efflux pump (Buroni et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buroni et al., 2006.

claim: De-repression of lfrA was shown to increase the MIC to ciprofloxacin 16-fold.
source: LfrA contributes to the intrinsic resistance of M. smegmatis to FQs (Takiff et al., 1996; Sander et al., 2000), and de-repression of lfrA was shown to increase the MIC to CIP 16-fold (Drusano, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Drusano, 2004.

claim: The isolated lfrR mutants had a mean 34-fold increase in IC50 to ciprofloxacin over wild-type.
source: The isolated lfrR mutants were significantly more resistant to CIP (mean 34-fold increase in IC50 over wild-type, Figure 1C), than the other 15 mutants (mean 7-fold increase, p=0.0003).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The 15 non-gyrA, non-lfrR mutants had a mean 7-fold increase in IC50 to ciprofloxacin.
source: The isolated lfrR mutants were significantly more resistant to CIP (mean 34-fold increase in IC50 over wild-type, Figure 1C), than the other 15 mutants (mean 7-fold increase, p=0.0003).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 14 of 15 non-gyrA, non-lfrR mutants had mutations within genes associated with the ribosome.
source: When we examined the genome sequence of the 15 non-gyrA, non-lfrR mutants, 14/15 had mutations within genes associated with the ribosome.
evidence: The claim is based on whole genome sequencing data.

claim: Ten ciprofloxacin-resistant mutants contained small insertions or deletions in operons encoding ribosomal proteins.
source: Ten contained small insertions or deletions in operons encoding ribosomal proteins (Figure 2A, Table 1), including seven with frameshift mutations in proteins composing the large ribosomal subunit: 5 in rplO (L15), 1 in rplF (L6), and 1 in rplY (L25).
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data presented in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: Seven ciprofloxacin-resistant mutants had frameshift mutations in proteins composing the large ribosomal subunit: 5 in rplO (L15), 1 in rplF (L6), and 1 in rplY (L25).
source: Ten contained small insertions or deletions in operons encoding ribosomal proteins (Figure 2A, Table 1), including seven with frameshift mutations in proteins composing the large ribosomal subunit: 5 in rplO (L15), 1 in rplF (L6), and 1 in rplY (L25).
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data presented in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: Two ciprofloxacin-resistant mutants had frameshifts in rpsE, encoding the S5 protein of the small subunit.
source: One mutant had an intergenic deletion between rplW and rplB (L23/L2), and two had frameshifts in rpsE, encoding the S5 protein of the small subunit.
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data.

claim: Four of the five remaining ciprofloxacin-resistant mutants had SNPs in rrlB (23S rRNA).
source: Four of the five remaining mutants had SNPs in rrlB (23S rRNA), one of two ribosomal RNA operons in M. smegmatis (Sander et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data.

claim: M. smegmatis has two ribosomal RNA operons.
source: Four of the five remaining mutants had SNPs in rrlB (23S rRNA), one of two ribosomal RNA operons in M. smegmatis (Sander et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sander et al., 1996.

claim: Engineering selected ribosomal mutations (rplO-1 and rpsE-1) into the chromosome of M. smegmatis using allelic exchange confirmed these mutations were directly responsible for the FQ-resistant phenotype.
source: We confirmed that these ribosomal mutations were directly responsible for FQ-resistant phenotype by engineering selected mutations (rplO-1 and rpsE-1; see Table 1) into the chromosome of M. smegmatis using allelic exchange (Figure 2B) and measuring the corresponding MICs to CIP.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from allelic exchange experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Complementation by a plasmid expressing a wild-type rplO allele restored CIP sensitivity to the rplO-1 mutant.
source: Complementation by a plasmid expressing a wild-type rplO allele restored CIP sensitivity to the rplO-1 mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ribosomal mutants showed cross-resistance to antibiotics of unrelated classes to which they had never been exposed.
source: Intriguingly, ribosomal mutants showed cross-resistance to antibiotics of unrelated classes to which they had never been exposed (Figure 2C), as well as collateral sensitivity to meropenem.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ribosomal mutants showed collateral sensitivity to meropenem.
source: Intriguingly, ribosomal mutants showed cross-resistance to antibiotics of unrelated classes to which they had never been exposed (Figure 2C), as well as collateral sensitivity to meropenem.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ribosomal mutants showed an average 40-fold increase in IC50 to isoniazid over wild-type (range 6.5 to 158-fold).
source: The most pronounced shifts were to the cell-wall biosynthesis inhibitor isoniazid (INH), with an average 40-fold increase in IC50 over wild-type (range 6.5 to 158-fold).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental measurements.

claim: lfrR mutants showed little cross-resistance to isoniazid.
source: In contrast, lfrR mutants showed little cross-resistance to INH, consistent with previous characterizations of this efflux system.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and is consistent with prior knowledge.

claim: Ribosomal mutants were better able to tolerate membrane stress due to SDS exposure compared to wild-type bacteria.
source: Ribosomal mutants were better able to tolerate membrane stress due to SDS exposure (Figure 2D) and high temperature (54°C, Figure 2E) compared to wild-type bacteria.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ribosomal mutants were better able to tolerate high temperature (54°C) compared to wild-type bacteria.
source: Ribosomal mutants were better able to tolerate membrane stress due to SDS exposure (Figure 2D) and high temperature (54°C, Figure 2E) compared to wild-type bacteria.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Ribosomal mutants had doubling times ranging from 4–6.5 hr, in contrast to the 2.4 hr doubling time of the parental wild-type strain or lfrR mutants.
source: In contrast to the 2.4 hr doubling time calculated for the parental wild-type strain or lfrR mutants, ribosomal mutants had doubling times ranging from 4–6.5 hr.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The slow growth of mutants generated via allelic exchange confirmed that the ribosomal lesions directly reduce growth rates.
source: The slow growth of mutants generated via allelic exchange confirmed that the ribosomal lesions directly reduce growth rates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from allelic exchange mutants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Slower growth rates alone did not recapitulate the IC50 shifts seen in the ribosomal mutants.
source: Slower growth rates alone did not recapitulate the IC50 shifts seen in the ribosomal mutants.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data comparing growth rates and antibiotic sensitivity.

claim: Growth rate was correlated with INH resistance (R² = 0.48) but weakly inversely correlated with CIP and novobiocin resistance (R² = 0.13, 0.14).
source: Although growth was correlated with INH resistance (R2 = 0.48) it was actually weakly inversely correlated with CIP and novobiocin (NOV) resistance (R2 = 0.13, 0.14), showing that the higher IC50s of the mutants are cannot be accounted for solely by their slower growth.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Only tetracycline significantly suppressed the activity of INH and CIP among the protein synthesis inhibitors tested.
source: Most protein synthesis inhibitors tested behaved additively with CIP or INH, thus ruling out general impairment of protein synthesis as the likely mechanism of resistance in these mutants. Only tetracycline significantly suppressed the activity of INH (Figure 3D) and CIP (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is based on checkerboard assay data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Tetracyclines act uniquely by inhibiting tRNA entry at the A-site.
source: Among the inhibitors tested, tetracyclines act uniquely by inhibiting tRNA entry at the A-site (Connell et al., 2003), suggesting that this step in protein synthesis may be a common impairment among our ribosomal mutants, and that the consequences of such impairment are transduced to produce multidrug resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Connell et al., 2003.

claim: All of the ribosomal mutants showed abundant transcriptional changes relative to the parent, with an average of 1023 of 6718 transcripts (15%) differentially expressed (range 471–2046).
source: All of the ribosomal mutants showed abundant changes relative to the parent; on average, 1023 of 6718 transcripts (15%) were differentially expressed (range 471–2046), and these changes were highly overlapping as demonstrated by a core set of 227 genes that were significantly regulated in all nine ribosomal mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAseq data analysis.

claim: A core set of 227 genes were significantly regulated in all nine ribosomal mutants.
source: All of the ribosomal mutants showed abundant changes relative to the parent; on average, 1023 of 6718 transcripts (15%) were differentially expressed (range 471–2046), and these changes were highly overlapping as demonstrated by a core set of 227 genes that were significantly regulated in all nine ribosomal mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Of the 407 genes differentially regulated in the lfrR mutant, only 12 were among the core 227 shared by all ribosomal mutants.
source: In contrast, of the 407 genes that were differentially regulated in the lfrR mutant, only 12 were among the core 227 shared by all of the ribosomal mutants.
evidence: The claim is based on RNAseq data analysis.

claim: The overlap between changes in proteome of the rplO-1 mutant showed moderate correlation with the transcriptomic changes observed by RNAseq (Pearson = 0.55, p<0.001).
source: The overlap between the changes in proteome of the rplO-1 mutant showed moderate correlation with the transcriptomic changes observed by RNAseq (Pearson = 0.55, p<0.001, Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of iTRAQ and RNAseq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: iTRAQ revealed a reduction in the ratio of large ribosomal subunit proteins relative to small subunit proteins in the rplO-1 mutant that was not reflected in the transcriptomic data.
source: iTRAQ revealed a reduction in the ratio of large ribosomal subunit proteins relative to small subunit proteins (Figure 4C) that was not reflected in the transcriptomic data, suggesting that the ribosomal mutations might have an effect on the stability or assembly of the large subunit, either decreasing its rate of translation or increasing its rate of degradation.
evidence: The claim is based on iTRAQ proteomic data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The profiles of ribosomal mutants indicate a marked increase in the individual 30S and 50S units and a corresponding decrease in fully assembled 70S subunits relative to the parent.
source: Indeed, the profiles of the mutants indicate a marked increase in the individual 30S and 50S units and a corresponding decrease in fully assembled 70S subunits relative to the parent (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on sucrose gradient ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mistranslated peptides were not more relatively abundant in the rplO-1 mutant compared to the parent, indicating mistranslation is unlikely to contribute to resistance.
source: However, the mean and median ratios seen in the mistranslated peptides are no different than the ratios seen across the larger set of 'normal' peptide; thus, mistranslated, antibiotic-insensitive targets are unlikely to contribute to resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of proteomic data for mistranslated peptides.

claim: MSMEG_6384 (katG) transcript levels were reduced 7.1-fold in the rplO-1 mutant (adjusted p-value=1.0×10^-54).
source: Relative to the parent strain. levels of katG transcript were reduced 7.1-fold in the rplO-1 mutant (adjusted p-value=1.0×10−54) and in all of the other ribosomal mutants (average of 3.9-fold across all of the mutants, minimum 2.5-fold, adjusted p-value=1.1×10−13), while iTRAQ showed a 4.2-fold reduction at the protein level in the rplO-1 mutant.
evidence: The claim is based on RNAseq data.

claim: katG transcript levels were reduced in all ribosomal mutants with an average of 3.9-fold across all mutants (minimum 2.5-fold, adjusted p-value=1.1×10^-13).
source: Relative to the parent strain. levels of katG transcript were reduced 7.1-fold in the rplO-1 mutant (adjusted p-value=1.0×10−54) and in all of the other ribosomal mutants (average of 3.9-fold across all of the mutants, minimum 2.5-fold, adjusted p-value=1.1×10−13), while iTRAQ showed a 4.2-fold reduction at the protein level in the rplO-1 mutant.
evidence: The claim is based on RNAseq data.

claim: iTRAQ showed a 4.2-fold reduction in KatG protein levels in the rplO-1 mutant.
source: Relative to the parent strain. levels of katG transcript were reduced 7.1-fold in the rplO-1 mutant (adjusted p-value=1.0×10−54) and in all of the other ribosomal mutants (average of 3.9-fold across all of the mutants, minimum 2.5-fold, adjusted p-value=1.1×10−13), while iTRAQ showed a 4.2-fold reduction at the protein level in the rplO-1 mutant.
evidence: The claim is based on iTRAQ proteomic data.

claim: KatG is required for converting the prodrug INH to its active form.
source: Among the genes and gene products underexpressed in all strains by RNAseq and also in the iTRAQ dataset was MSMEG_6384, encoding the catalase KatG, which is required for converting the prodrug INH to its active form Zhang et al. (1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 1992.

claim: INH sensitivity was restored in the rplO-1 mutant background solely by restoring KatG levels back to wild-type levels.
source: Indeed, INH sensitivity was restored in the mutant background solely by restoring KatG levels back to wild-type levels, (Figure 4E), suggesting that INH resistance is due to the perturbations in KatG levels caused by the ribosomal mutations on the transcriptome and subsequently, on the proteome.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: WhiB7 was one of the most highly induced proteins in the rplO-1 mutant (6.0-fold, adjusted p-value=2.5×10^-4) as measured by iTRAQ.
source: As measured by iTRAQ, WhiB7 was one of the most highly induced proteins (6.0-fold, adjusted p-value=2.5×10−4) and by RNAseq, whiB7 mRNA was up 7.4-fold in rplO-1 relative to the parent strain (p adj.=4.4×10104) and in all of the other ribosomal mutants (average of 3.2-fold; minimum 1.7-fold, adjusted p-value=2.1×10−6).
evidence: The claim is based on iTRAQ proteomic data.

claim: whiB7 mRNA was up 7.4-fold in rplO-1 relative to the parent strain (p adj.=4.4×10^-104) by RNAseq.
source: As measured by iTRAQ, WhiB7 was one of the most highly induced proteins (6.0-fold, adjusted p-value=2.5×10−4) and by RNAseq, whiB7 mRNA was up 7.4-fold in rplO-1 relative to the parent strain (p adj.=4.4×10104) and in all of the other ribosomal mutants (average of 3.2-fold; minimum 1.7-fold, adjusted p-value=2.1×10−6).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAseq data.

claim: whiB7 mRNA was upregulated in all ribosomal mutants with an average of 3.2-fold (minimum 1.7-fold, adjusted p-value=2.1×10^-6).
source: As measured by iTRAQ, WhiB7 was one of the most highly induced proteins (6.0-fold, adjusted p-value=2.5×10−4) and by RNAseq, whiB7 mRNA was up 7.4-fold in rplO-1 relative to the parent strain (p adj.=4.4×10104) and in all of the other ribosomal mutants (average of 3.2-fold; minimum 1.7-fold, adjusted p-value=2.1×10−6).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAseq data.

claim: WhiB7 is a transcription factor conserved throughout the actinomycetes that positively regulates genes that contribute to innate antibiotic resistance.
source: Similarly, we noted that among the global transcriptomic and proteomic changes occurring in the mutants, the induction of WhiB7, a transcription factor conserved throughout the actinomycetes that positively regulates genes that contribute to innate antibiotic resistance, was among one of the strongest signals.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about WhiB7 function.

claim: In M. smegmatis, whiB7 has been shown to be highly induced after exposure to specific classes of protein synthesis inhibitors, particularly tetracyclines and macrolides.
source: In M. smegmatis, whiB7 has been shown to be highly induced after exposure to specific classes of protein synthesis inhibitors, particularly tetracyclines and macrolides (Burian et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Burian et al., 2012.

claim: Deletion of whiB7 in the rplO-1 background restored sensitivity to CIP, ethionamide (ETH) and cycloserine (CYC).
source: In the rplO-1 background, deletion of whiB7 restored sensitivity to a CIP, ethionamide (ETH) and cycloserine (CYC) (Figure 4C), indicating a critical role for WhiB7 in the broad-spectrum resistance observed in the rplO-1 mutant.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from whiB7 deletion mutants shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Deletion of whiB7 did not fully restore INH sensitivity to rplO-1, nor did it alleviate the increased sensitivity to meropenem.
source: Deletion of whiB7 however, did not fully restore INH sensitivity to rplO-1, nor did it alleviate the increased sensitivity to meropenem.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from whiB7 deletion mutants.

claim: Constitutive expression of WhiB7 at a high-level from a plasmid in a wild-type background did not confer resistance to CIP, INH, ETH, or MER.
source: We then constitutively expressed WhiB7 at a high-level from a plasmid in a wild-type background and found that it alone did not confer resistance to CIP, INH, ETH, or MER (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ribosomal mutants arose during double selection in CIP and INH at a 3600-fold higher frequency (5.5 × 10^-7) than the product of their frequencies in CIP (1.5 × 10^-5) and INH (1.0 × 10^-5) alone.
source: Mutants arose during double selection at a 3600-fold higher frequency (5.5 × 10−7) than the product of their frequencies in CIP (1.5 × 10−5) and INH (1.0 × 10−5) alone, suggesting that the mutants that arose in the presence of both CIP and INH are not the product of two completely uncoupled mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from double selection experiments.

claim: Two mutants that arose under double selection in CIP and INH had the same frameshift mutations in rplO previously observed in rplO-2 (77ΔA) and rplO-3 (74-77ΔGTGA).
source: When we PCR amplified and sequenced a fragment including the rplF, rpsE and rplO genes from three mutants that arose under double selection, we identified the same frameshift mutations in rplO in two of these that we had previously observed in rplO-2 (77ΔA) and rplO-3 (74-77ΔGTGA).
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data from mutants selected in both CIP and INH.

claim: Upon selection at 3.5 µg/ml CIP, strains with mutations in rplO or rplF yielded 10–100 fold more high-level CIP resistant mutants per input cell than wild-type cells.
source: In support of this, we found that upon selection at 3.5 µg/ml CIP, a bactericidal concentration for both wild-type cells and the ribosomal mutants (Figure 5B), strains with mutations in rplO or rplF yielded 10–100 fold more high-level CIP resistant mutants per input cell than wild-type cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Secondary mutations in both gyrA and lfrR were identified in high-level CIP resistant mutants derived from ribosomal mutants.
source: When we sequenced the gyrA and lfrR loci in these mutants, secondary mutations in both of these genes were identified (Table 2, strains rplO-lfrR-1 through six and rplO-gyrA-1).
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data presented in Table 2.

claim: Serial passage of three parallel cultures of the rplO-1 mutant in antibiotic-free medium resulted in wild-type growth rates by passage 12.
source: We serially passaged three parallel cultures of the rplO-1 mutant in antibiotic-free medium. By passage 12, cultures demonstrated wild-type growth rates (Figure 5D) as well as wild-type sensitivities to CIP and INH (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from serial passage experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Evolved strains from serial passage of rplO-1 in all three cultures had acquired an additional insertion or deletion at the rplO locus, restoring the wild-type reading frame.
source: Evolved strains in all three cultures had acquired an additional insertion or deletion at the rplO locus (Figure 5F, Table 2), restoring the wild-type reading frame but leaving short deletions or coding changes in the region between the two sequential mutations.
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data shown in Figure 5F and Table 2.

claim: Reversion to wild-type growth rates can occur readily in a rplO gyrA double mutant during continued passage at 3.5 µg/ml CIP.
source: We then demonstrated that reversion to wild-type growth rates can also occur readily in a rplO gyrA double mutant (rplO-1 gyrA-1, Table 2) during continued passage at 3.5 µg/ml CIP (Figure 5G–H, Table 2); INH resistance is lost as a consequence of a compensatory one base insertion that restores the original reading frame but alters one codon in rplO.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 5G-H and Table 2.

claim: The majority (19/23 clones) from well A-G20 had only the rrlB C904A mutation.
source: While the majority (19/23 clones) had only the rrlB C904A mutation, three had both the rrlB C904A and lfrR T452C mutation.
evidence: The claim is based on PCR characterization data presented in Table 3.

claim: Three clones from well A-G20 had both the rrlB C904A and lfrR T452C mutation.
source: While the majority (19/23 clones) had only the rrlB C904A mutation, three had both the rrlB C904A and lfrR T452C mutation.
evidence: The claim is based on PCR characterization data presented in Table 3.

claim: One clone from well A-G20 had the rrlB C904A mutation paired with a different lfrR allele, 63(+C).
source: Surprisingly, the final clone had the rrlB C904A mutation paired with a different lfrR allele, 63(+C).
evidence: The claim is based on PCR characterization data presented in Table 3.

claim: The rrlB C904A mutation likely arose first in well A-G20, enabling slow replication in the presence of CIP.
source: Thus, the rrlB C904A mutation likely arose first, enabling slow replication in the presence of CIP and accounting for the delayed emergence of well A-G20 on day 5.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the distribution of mutations in clones from well A-G20.

claim: Ribosomal mutations do not result in mistranslation.
source: In summary, the ribosomal mutations, while impairing 70S assembly, do not appear to lead to mistranslation; nevertheless, they cause an overall stress to the cell that results in a major reprogramming of the transcriptome and proteome of the bacteria, that ultimately lead to a multi-drug resistant phenotype.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of proteomic data for mistranslated peptides.

claim: Ribosomal mutations impair 70S ribosome assembly.
source: In summary, the ribosomal mutations, while impairing 70S assembly, do not appear to lead to mistranslation; nevertheless, they cause an overall stress to the cell that results in a major reprogramming of the transcriptome and proteome of the bacteria, that ultimately lead to a multi-drug resistant phenotype.
evidence: The claim is based on sucrose gradient ultracentrifugation data.

claim: Ribosomal mutations cause an overall stress to the cell that results in a major reprogramming of the transcriptome and proteome of the bacteria.
source: In summary, the ribosomal mutations, while impairing 70S assembly, do not appear to lead to mistranslation; nevertheless, they cause an overall stress to the cell that results in a major reprogramming of the transcriptome and proteome of the bacteria, that ultimately lead to a multi-drug resistant phenotype.
evidence: The claim is based on RNAseq and iTRAQ data showing widespread transcriptomic and proteomic changes.

claim: Among the non-essential ribosomal proteins in E. coli and B. subtilis are L15 (RplO) and L25 (RplY), which were identified in this study as playing a role in multidrug resistance.
source: Among these non-essential proteins are two identified in this study that can play a role in multidrug resistance, namely L15 (RplO) and L25 (RplY).
evidence: The claim is based on prior studies of gene essentiality and the findings of this study.

claim: L6 (RplF) and S5 (RpsE) are essential ribosomal proteins in E. coli and B. subtilis.
source: The other ribosomal proteins identified in our study, L6 (RplF) and S5 (RpsE), are essential in these organisms.
evidence: The claim is based on prior studies of gene essentiality cited in the text.

claim: rplF and rpsE are essential in M. tuberculosis.
source: Transposon-based studies of gene essentiality in the related mycobacterium M. tuberculosis (Sassetti et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2012) show that rplF and rplE are also essential in M. tuberculosis, while rplY was non-essential and the essentiality of rplO was indeterminate.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sassetti et al., 2003 and Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: The mutations found in rplF and rpsE occur near the 3' end of the open reading frames, leaving the majority of the corresponding proteins, L6 and S5, unaltered.
source: The mutations we found in rplF and rpsE occur near the 3' end of the open reading frames, leaving the majority of the corresponding proteins, L6 and S5 unaltered.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the sequencing data showing the location of mutations.

claim: Tetracycline's primary binding site is located near the A site, where it interacts with 16S RNA in the 30S subunit.
source: Although tetracycline binds to the ribosome at several locations (Day, 1966), its primary binding site is located near the A site, where it interacts with 16S RNA in the 30S subunit (Brodersen et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Day, 1966 and Brodersen et al., 2000.

claim: At its primary binding site, tetracycline inhibits protein synthesis by interfering with tRNA entry.
source: At this site, tetracycline inhibits protein synthesis by interfering with tRNA entry (Wurmbach and Nierhaus, 1983; Maxwell, 1967).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wurmbach and Nierhaus, 1983 and Maxwell, 1967.

claim: The ribosomal mutations identified may have subtle effects in translation initiation that are similar to the effects of low concentrations of tetracycline.
source: Thus, the ribosomal mutations we have identified may have subtle effects in translation initiation that are similar to the effects of low concentrations of tetracycline.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the drug interaction experiments showing tetracycline uniquely phenocopies the ribosomal mutations.

claim: The slower growth rates of natural isolates of E. coli were shown to be well-correlated with the kinetic properties of their ribosomes.
source: While traditional culture conditions in the laboratory select for strains with ribosomal properties that maximize growth rates, the varied environments encountered by microbes in nature may select for other ribosomal properties; the slower growth rates of natural isolates of E. coli were shown to be well-correlated with the kinetic properties of their ribosomes, and extended axenic culture of these isolates led to the evolution of culture-adapted strains with growth rates similar to those seen in laboratory strains (Mikkola and Kurland, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mikkola and Kurland, 1991.

claim: Extended axenic culture of natural E. coli isolates led to the evolution of culture-adapted strains with growth rates similar to those seen in laboratory strains.
source: While traditional culture conditions in the laboratory select for strains with ribosomal properties that maximize growth rates, the varied environments encountered by microbes in nature may select for other ribosomal properties; the slower growth rates of natural isolates of E. coli were shown to be well-correlated with the kinetic properties of their ribosomes, and extended axenic culture of these isolates led to the evolution of culture-adapted strains with growth rates similar to those seen in laboratory strains (Mikkola and Kurland, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mikkola and Kurland, 1991.

claim: Ribosomal mutations can serve as stepping-stones in an evolutionary path leading to the emergence of high-level, multidrug resistance.
source: Such transient mutations can thus serve as stepping-stones that facilitate evolution from antibiotic sensitivity to multidrug resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing ribosomal mutants can acquire high-level resistance mutations and then revert.

claim: Suppressor mutations can be easily acquired to restore wild-type growth in ribosomal mutants.
source: Further, suppressor mutations can then be easily acquired to restore wild-type growth.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing reversion of growth defects through additional mutations.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding ribosomal components in M. smegmatis confer resistance to several structurally and mechanistically unrelated classes of antibiotics.
source: We have identified mutations in genes encoding ribosomal components in Mycobacterium smegmatis that confer resistance to several structurally and mechanistically unrelated classes of antibiotics and enhance survival following heat shock and membrane stress.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing cross-resistance to multiple antibiotics.

claim: Ribosomal mutations enhance survival following heat shock and membrane stress.
source: We have identified mutations in genes encoding ribosomal components in Mycobacterium smegmatis that confer resistance to several structurally and mechanistically unrelated classes of antibiotics and enhance survival following heat shock and membrane stress.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Ribosomal mutations affect ribosome assembly.
source: These mutations affect ribosome assembly and cause large-scale transcriptomic and proteomic changes, including the downregulation of the catalase KatG, an activating enzyme required for isoniazid sensitivity, and upregulation of WhiB7, a transcription factor involved in innate antibiotic resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on sucrose gradient ultracentrifugation data.

claim: Ribosomal mutations cause large-scale transcriptomic and proteomic changes.
source: These mutations affect ribosome assembly and cause large-scale transcriptomic and proteomic changes, including the downregulation of the catalase KatG, an activating enzyme required for isoniazid sensitivity, and upregulation of WhiB7, a transcription factor involved in innate antibiotic resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on RNAseq and iTRAQ data.

claim: Ribosomal mutations cause downregulation of the catalase KatG, an activating enzyme required for isoniazid sensitivity.
source: These mutations affect ribosome assembly and cause large-scale transcriptomic and proteomic changes, including the downregulation of the catalase KatG, an activating enzyme required for isoniazid sensitivity, and upregulation of WhiB7, a transcription factor involved in innate antibiotic resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on RNAseq and iTRAQ data showing reduced KatG levels.

claim: Ribosomal mutations cause upregulation of WhiB7, a transcription factor involved in innate antibiotic resistance.
source: These mutations affect ribosome assembly and cause large-scale transcriptomic and proteomic changes, including the downregulation of the catalase KatG, an activating enzyme required for isoniazid sensitivity, and upregulation of WhiB7, a transcription factor involved in innate antibiotic resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on RNAseq and iTRAQ data showing increased WhiB7 levels.

claim: M. smegmatis mc2155 was obtained from Keith Derbyshire at the University of Albany.
source: Mycobacterium smegmatis mc2155 was obtained from Keith Derbyshire at the University of Albany.
evidence: The claim states the source of the bacterial strain used in the study.

claim: Approximately 10^5 cells are required for a fluorescent signal 10 units above background.
source: Approximately 105 cells are required for a signal 10 units above background.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental calibration data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.
